idiom_name: Subject interface + proxy class holding a reference to the real subject
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: define (or reuse) the Subject interface, implement the real subject behind it, then write a Proxy that also implements Subject, holds a reference to the real subject (or the information needed to obtain it), and performs its policy - create-on-demand, permission check, cache lookup, reference counting, marshalling - before forwarding the call unchanged. Clients depend only on Subject and receive the proxy from a factory or creation method, so the choice of proxy versus real subject stays out of the call sites. Keep the forwarding faithful: same parameters, same exceptions, same order of side effects; lifecycle, caching and transport are the proxy's private business.
code_sketch:
interface Subject:  op() -> Result

class RealSubject(Subject): op() -> ...      # the real work
class Proxy(Subject):
    def op(self):
        self.ensure_real()                   # policy: create/authorize/cache
        return self.real.op()                # forward unchanged

client(Subject p): p.op()                    # cannot tell proxy from real
pitfalls: A proxy that changes the interface or the semantics is an Adapter or a Decorator in disguise; keep the substitution faithful.
The proxy must own the decision of when the real subject is created and released, or lifecycle bugs leak across the boundary.
If the real subject stays directly reachable, protection proxies are advisory only.
Caching before authorization: a proxy that memoizes results before checking permissions can leak cached data to unauthorized callers.
Timeout stacking in remote proxies: outer timeouts short-circuit inner timeouts, making it impossible to distinguish a slow downstream from a misconfigured timeout budget.
Proxy recursion: a proxy that calls a method on itself instead of the next in the chain, caused by incorrect self-wiring or missing unwrap/getTarget guards.
Schema/version drift in remote proxies: the proxy serializes with one schema version while the remote service expects another, causing silent data corruption or hard-to-debug parse failures.
Cache stampedes: concurrent requests all miss the cache simultaneously, all hit the real subject, overwhelming it before the first response is cached.
Negative caching mistakes: caching null or error results and returning them on subsequent requests, masking transient failures that would recover on retry.
Silent exception swallowing: a proxy catches and discards exceptions, changing the observable contract so callers cannot distinguish success from failure.
Wrong move: compare proxy and target by object identity -> set/map behavior diverges -> instead define and test canonical equality/hash semantics across both representations.
Wrong move: publish the real subject beside its protection proxy -> callers bypass checks -> instead make the proxy the only capability handed to clients.
Wrong move: let each proxy layer set a full remote timeout -> outer deadlines mask downstream behavior -> instead carry one deadline and budget each hop explicitly.
